title: Onion Tomato Chutney: The 20-Minute South Indian Staple Every Kitchen Needs
excerpt: A simple, balanced condiment made with equal parts onions and tomatoes, this chutney pairs with everything from crispy dosa to steamed rice.
body:
• Onion tomato chutney is a staple South Indian condiment made with equal parts onions and tomatoes, urad dal, dried red chilies, and a touch of tamarind — ready in about 20 minutes.
  • The chutney pairs with dosa, idli, medu vada, and uttapam, and can double as a sandwich spread or dip for savory snacks.
  • Every South Indian household has its own version; the key is cooking the tomatoes fully and not burning the urad dal, which would make the chutney bitter.

In the rotation of South Indian breakfast chutneys — coconut, peanut, ginger, tomato — onion tomato chutney occupies a quiet but essential place. It is the one you make when you want something quick, balanced, and versatile enough to go with whatever is on the breakfast plate.

Unlike coconut chutney, which requires fresh coconut, or peanut chutney, which leans heavily on roasted nuts, onion tomato chutney relies on two of the most universally available ingredients in an Indian kitchen. Equal parts onions and tomatoes, a small measure of urad dal for body, dried red chilies for heat, and a piece of tamarind for brightness. That is the whole recipe.

How It Comes Together

The process starts with toasting half a teaspoon of urad dal in a tablespoon of oil over low heat until it turns light golden. One or two dried red chilies go in next. The dal needs to brown evenly without blackening — burnt lentils or chilies make the chutney irreversibly bitter.

"How It Comes Together The process starts with toasting half a teaspoon of urad dal in a tablespoon of oil over low heat until it turns light golden."

A cup of chopped onions (about 100 grams) follows, sautéed until softened and lightly golden. Then an equal weight of chopped tomatoes, a pinch of asafoetida, and salt. The tomatoes cook until they collapse entirely and lose their raw smell, a step that separates a smooth, rounded chutney from one that tastes unfinished.

Once cooled, everything goes into a grinder with a small piece of seedless tamarind. Blend smooth without water if possible; add a few tablespoons only if needed. The result is a thick, vibrant chutney with a gentle sweetness from the onions, pleasant tang from the tomatoes, and a subtle sour note from the tamarind that ties everything together.

The Tempering Question

Many home cooks skip the tempering entirely, and the chutney holds its own without it. The sautéed onions and dal provide enough flavor depth. But for a weekend breakfast or when serving guests, a quick tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves, and a broken dried red chili poured over the chutney adds a layer of aroma and crackle.

Where It Belongs on the Table

Onion tomato chutney is a natural companion to the full South Indian tiffin spread: crispy dosa, soft idli, medu vada, uttapam, paniyaram, ragi dosa, and adai. It works alongside coconut chutney rather than replacing it — the two offer contrasting flavors that complement each other.

Beyond breakfast, it serves as a spread for sandwiches and wraps, or as a dip for fried snacks like potato bajji, mysore bonda, and goli baje. Served with a plate of steamed rice, sambar, and rasam, it rounds out a full South Indian meal.

Regional Variations and Storage

Every household adjusts the ratio to taste. Some lean heavier on tomatoes for extra tang; others use more onions for sweetness. Sesame oil (gingelly oil) instead of a neutral oil adds an earthier, more traditional flavor, particularly in Tamil Nadu and parts of Andhra Pradesh. The tamarind is optional — if the tomatoes are already tart, it can be skipped.

The chutney keeps for up to one day in an airtight container in the refrigerator. It may thicken after chilling; stir in a little water before serving. For the freshest flavor, it is best eaten the day it is made.

Nutrition at a Glance

A serving runs roughly 67 calories, with 6 grams of carbohydrates, 5 grams of fat, and 1 gram of protein. It provides 7 milligrams of vitamin C and 324 IU of vitamin A — modest numbers, but the chutney functions as a flavor vehicle, not a nutritional centerpiece.
